# R Syntax

## 1
_Insert the missing part of the code below to output "Hello World!"._
```{r syntax_1, cache=TRUE}
"Hello, World!"
```
Added quotes to make it a string.

## 2
_In R, you can also use a function to output code. Fill in the missing part to output "Hello World!":_
```{r syntax_2, cache=TRUE}
print("Hello, World!")
```
`print()` feels more similar to other programming language syntax.

## 3
_Comments in R are written with a special character. Insert the missing part:_
```{r syntax_3, cache=TRUE}
# This is a comment
"Hello World!"
```
How meta...

# R Variables

## 1
_Create a variable named carName and assign the value Volvo to it._
```{r variables_1, cache=TRUE}
carName <- "Volvo"
```
Arrows point the direction of flow.

## 2
_Create a variable named maxSpeed and assign the value 120 to it._
```{r variables_2, cache=TRUE}
maxSpeed <- 120
```
Numeric values do not need quotes, they are not strings.

## 3
_Use the correct function to combine the text "Hello" with the txt variable, to output "Hello World!"._
```{r variables_3, cache=TRUE}
txt <- "World!"
paste("Hello", txt)
```
`paste()` combines strings with a space by default.

## 4
_Display the sum of 5 + 10, using two variables: x and y._
```{r variables_4, cache=TRUE}
x <- 5
y <- 10
x + y
```
Simple arithmetic with variables, pretty straightforward.

## 5
_Assign the value "Orange" to multiple variables in one line:_
```{r variables_5, cache=TRUE}
fruit1 <- fruit2 <- fruit3 <- "Orange"
```
Chained assignment works in R, pretty nifty!

# R Data Types

## 1
_What data type is myVar?_
```{r datatypes_1, cache=TRUE}
myVar <- 30
class(myVar)
```
`class()` is similar to `type()` in Python or `typeof()` in JavaScript. It should show that myVar is of type "numeric".

## 2
_Which function can be used to check the data type of a variable?_
```{r datatypes_2, cache=TRUE}
x <- 10.5
class(x)
```
Same as above, `class()` reveals the data type.

## 1
_Use the correct function to find the lowest number in a set._
```{r math_1, cache=TRUE}
min(5, 10, 15)
```
`min()` is pretty self explanatory, find the minimum!

```{r math_2, cache=TRUE}
sqrt(16)
```
`sqrt()`, again, self explanatory.

# R Strings

## 1
_Create a str variable with the value "Hello":_
```{r strings_1, cache=TRUE}
str <- "Hello"
```
Repeat of [R Variables > 1](#r-variables).

## 2
_Use the correct function to find the number of characters in the str variable:_
```{r strings_2, cache=TRUE}
str <- "Hello World!"
nchar(str)
```
`nchar()`= `n`umber of `char`acters. Why does R use `nchar` when nearly every other language uses `length` or similar? That's R for you.

## 3
_Use the correct function to check if the character "H" is present in the str variable:_
```{r strings_3, cache=TRUE}
str <- "Hello World!"
grepl("H", str)
```
Another one that feels very R-specific, though I do appreciate the unix `grep` heritage.

## 4
_Use a function to combine concatenate the two strings:_
```{r strings_4, cache=TRUE}
str1 <- "Hello"
str2 <- "World!"
paste(str1, str2)
```
Repeat of [R Variables > 3](#r-variables).

# R Booleans

## 1
_What is the output of the following code?_
```{r booleans_1, cache=TRUE}
10 < 9
```
FALSE, because 10 is not less than 9.

## 2
_Fill in the missing part to compare the two variables:_
```{r booleans_2, cache=TRUE}
a <- 10
b <- 9
a > b
```
10 is greater than 9 (at least for now).

## 3
_Fill in the missing part to print the value TRUE:_
```{r booleans_3, cache=TRUE}
a <- 10
b <- 9

a != b
```
There\'s `>`, `>=`, `!=`... a few options here.

# R Operators

## 1
_Multiply 10 with 5:_
```{r operators_1, cache=TRUE}
10 * 5
```
Simple multiplication operator, just like every other language.

## 2
_Divide 10 by 5:_
```{r operators_2, cache=TRUE}
10 / 5
```


# R If ... Else

## 1
_Print "Hello World" if `a` is greater than `b`._
```{r ifelse_1, cache=TRUE}
a <- 50
b <- 10
if (a > b) {
  print("Hello World")
}
```
Syntax is more like JavaScript or C here, with parentheses around the condition and curly braces for the block.

## 2
_Print "Hello World" if `a` is equal to `b`._
```{r ifelse_2, cache=TRUE}
a <- 50
b <- 50
if (a == b) {
  print("Hello World")
}
```
Same as above, just checking for equality.

## 3
_Print "Yes" if `a` is equal to `b`, otherwise print "No"._
```{r ifelse_3, cache=TRUE}
a <- 50
b <- 50
if (a == b) {
  print("Yes")
} else {
  print("No")
}
```
Again, pretty standard structure. 

# R Loops

## 1
_Print `i` as long as `i` is less than 6._
```{r loops_1, cache=TRUE}
i <- 1
while (i < 6) {
  print(i)
  i <- i + 1
}
```
`For` question one, use `while`. Don't forget to increment `i` (or you'll be stuck forever...)!

## 2
_Use the correct keyword to exit the loop if `i` is equal to 4._
```{r loops_2, cache=TRUE}
i <- 1
while (i < 6) {
    print(i)
    i <- i + 1
    if (i == 4) {
      break
    }
}
```
Are you ready to `break` out of this assignment grading loop, professor?

## 3
_Use the correct keyword to skip the value of 3 in a loop._
```{r loops_3, cache=TRUE}
i <- 0
while (i < 6) {
  i <- i + 1
  if (i == 3) {
    next
  }
  print(i)
}
```
`next` is pretty unique syntax to R, like Python's `continue`.

## 4
_Use the correct keyword to iterate over a sequence of numbers._
```{r loops_4, cache=TRUE}
for (x in 1:10) {
    print(x)
}
```
`While` iterating over a finite sequence, use `for`.

# R Functions

## 1
_Insert the missing parts to create a function with the name `my_function`._
```{r functions_1, cache=TRUE}
my_function <- function() {
  print("Hello World!")
}
```
Storing functions as a variable, more like JavaScript than Python in syntax.

## 2
_Insert the missing part to __call__ `my_function`._
```{r functions_2, cache=TRUE}
my_function <- function() {
  print("Hello World!")
}
my_function()
```
The parentheses function as an indicator of a `function()`.

## 3
_Add a `fname` argument to the function._
```{r functions_3, cache=TRUE}
my_function <- function(fname) {
    paste(fname)
}
my_function("Peter")
```
Pass in those arguments! On-the-fly function-scoped variables.

## 4
_Insert the missing part to return a result (15)._ 
```{r functions_4, cache=TRUE}
my_function <- function(x) {
    return(5 * x)
}
print(my_function(3))
```
`return()` is explicit in R, just like Python and JavaScript. I'm passing in the 3, and getting back the outpus specified in the `return` line.

# R Data Structures

## 1
_Insert the missing parts to create a vector of strings._ 
```{r datastructures_1, cache=TRUE}
fruits <- c("Banana", "Apple", "Orange")
```
It's time to `c`ombine some fruits into a vector!

## 2
_Insert the missing parts to find out how many items a vector has._ 
```{r datastructures_2, cache=TRUE}
fruits <- c("Banana", "Apple", "Orange")
length(fruits)
```
And `length` shows up here, on a vector. Why can't I use `length` on a string, only `nchar`? What is a string, but a vector of characters? Thanks, R.

## 3
_Insert the missing parts to create a list of strings._ 
```{r datastructures_3, cache=TRUE}
thislist <- list("Banana", "Apple", "Cherry")
```
This doesn't really do a good job showcasing why you'd use a list over a vector... Throw an integer in there.

## 4
_Insert the missing parts to create a matrix of strings._
```{r datastructures_4, cache=TRUE}
thismatrix <- matrix(c("Banana", "Apple", "Cherry", "Orange"), nrow=2, ncol=2)
```
Now that's a fruity spreadsheet.

## 5
_Insert the missing parts to create an array with two dimensions._
```{r datastructures_5, cache=TRUE}
thisarray <- c(1:24)
multiarray <- array(thisarray, dim = c(4,3,2))
```
Arrays remind me of working in MongoDB, just layers upon layers upon layers. Arrays of arrays of arrays. Something that bugs me with R is how much overlap there is between data structures. All of this could really be trimmed down like what we see in, say, JavaScript: arrays and objects. All of these R structure types are basically those two things, but it seems like they are trying to account for special rules, like limiting the contents to one data type. I get that R is specialized, but even so, some of these distinctions feel entirely unnecessary. Perhaps I'll feel differently as we go along.

## 6
_Insert the missing part to create a data frame._ 
```{r datastructures_6, cache=TRUE}
Data_Frame <<- data.frame(
    Training = c("Strength", "Stamina", "Other"),
    Pulse = c(100, 150, 120),
    Duration = c(60, 30, 45)
)
```
I'm changing this to be global so I can use it later in some plotting exercises.

## 7
_Insert the missing part to create a factor._ 
```{r datastructures_7, cache=TRUE}
music_genre <- factor(c("Jazz", "Rock", "Classic", "Classic", "Pop", "Jazz", "Rock", "Jazz"))
```
Factors, like buckets. For bucketing!

# R Graphics

## Plot
```{r graphics_plot, cache=TRUE, dependson="datastructures_6"}
plot(Data_Frame$Duration, Data_Frame$Pulse, type = "p", col = "blue", main = "Training Data", xlab = "Duration (minutes)", ylab = "Pulse (BPM)")
```
I thought I might as well use the `Data_Frame` from earlier and just create something new. I'm ignoring the "Training" categories, instead assuming that this is measuring pulse over the course of a single workout. What I get is a neat story of what I'm guessing is someone relaxing after a workout (however, 60 minutes and their bpm is STILL at 100? You may want to see a doctor.)

## Line
```{r graphics_line, cache=TRUE, dependson="datastructures_6"}
Data_Frame <- Data_Frame[order(Data_Frame$Duration), ]
plot(Data_Frame$Duration, Data_Frame$Pulse, type = "l", col = "blue", main = "Training Data", xlab = "Duration (minutes)", ylab = "Pulse (BPM)")
```
I had to reorder the data by Duration from low to high to get a proper line graph.

## Scatterplot
```{r graphics_scatterplot, cache=TRUE, dependson="datastructures_6"}
# day one, the age and speed of 12 cars:
x1 <- c(5,7,8,7,2,2,9,4,11,12,9,6)
y1 <- c(99,86,87,88,111,103,87,94,78,77,85,86)

# day two, the age and speed of 15 cars:
x2 <- c(2,2,8,1,15,8,12,9,7,3,11,4,7,14,12)
y2 <- c(100,105,84,105,90,99,90,95,94,100,79,112,91,80,85)

plot(x1, y1, main="Observation of Cars", xlab="Car age", ylab="Car speed", col = "green")
points(x2, y2, col = "red")
legend("topright", 
    legend = c("Day 1", "Day 2", "Trend"),
    col = c("green", "red", "blue"),
    lty = c(1,1,1),
    lwd = c(2,2,2)
)
# Trend line for car speed over time
model <- lm(c(y1, y2) ~ c(x1, x2))
abline(model, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
```
The example from the site, but with a legend now! And added a linear model trend line.

## Pie Charts
```{r graphics_pie, cache=TRUE, dependson="datastructures_6"}
pie(Data_Frame$Duration, label = Data_Frame$Training, main = "Training Duration Distribution")
```
Back to the training data. This was really easy, just the number value as x and label in the y position.

## Bars
```{r graphics_bars, cache=TRUE, dependson="datastructures_6"}
barplot(Data_Frame$Duration, names.arg = Data_Frame$Training, main = "Training Duration Distribution", density = 30)
```
Same as pie chart, really. Pretty easy to swap.

# R Statistics
I've got no datasets on hand, but I'd like to try my hand at making some. Looks like I can use `roxygen2` to generate Rd files, but making them by hand doesn't look too bad. I appreciate that R packages require all exported functions and datasets to have complete documentation.

I also like their use of `which()` in the examples, reminds me of oldschool `HLOOKUP`/`VLOOKUP` in Excel and fetching values before `XLOOKUP` became a thing. `rownames(Data_Cars)[which.max(Data_Cars$hp)]` is fairly elegant.

Cool that quartiles are the default on `quantile()`, quite easy.
